steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper presenting ZipIt!, our method for merging models trained on different tasks into a single multitask model without retraining. Motivate the problem, cover prior model merging work and its limits, explain our two main ideas, and summarize the experiments.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Progress of deep learning in vision and ever larger models
- Problem: expanding an existing model's capabilities
- Prior model merging work and its same-task limitation
- Idea 1: merging features within and across models, not just permutation
- Idea 2: partial zipping
- ZipIt! and its experimental validation

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Deep learning in vision
  - AlexNet (cite) popularized it; since then massive models, ever increasing number of parameters
  - once difficult/impossible problems now benchmarks: classification w/ tens of thousands of classes (cite), fast instance segmentation (cite), realistic image generation (cite)
- Expanding an existing model's capabilities
  - abundance of independent, carefully tuned models for many tasks
  - train on additional task -> catastrophic forgetting (cite)
  - same model on different data w/o adaptation -> doesn't generalize to out of domain samples (cite)
  - "intervention" strategies (cite) mitigate, but need further training, expensive (cite)
  - want: "zip" with models trained on the new tasks, no additional training
- Prior model merging
  - gaining traction in vision community
  - Model Soups (cite): add models finetuned from same pretrained init; better accuracy, robustness
  - Git Re-Basin (cite): same data, different inits; significant accuracy drop
  - REPAIR (cite): improves Git Re-Basin; new parameters, adjusts batch norms where applicable
  - all only combine models trained on the same task
  - ours: logical extreme, differently initialized models on completely separate tasks (Fig. 1 ab); incredibly difficult for prior work; two simple strategies
- Strategy 1: beyond permutation
  - prior work permutes one model to the other -> 1-1 mapping, assumes most features correlated
  - not necessarily true for different tasks -> permutation alone not enough
  - generalize merging: "zip" any combination of correlated features within and across each model
  - up to 20% better than permutation-based approaches on some tasks
  - proof: merging within models better, theoretical setting of earlier work (cite)
- Strategy 2: partial zipping
  - existing methods merge entire network; ok for extremely similar models, same setting
  - disjoint tasks: features less correlated over the course of the network (cite)
  - zip only up to a specified layer; merged outputs -> remaining unmerged layers of original networks; multi-head model
  - over 15% better depending on task difficulty, most layers still merged
- ZipIt! (Fig. 1 c)
  - zip any number of models from different tasks into one multitask model, no retraining
  - general graph-based algorithm for merging and unmerging (Sec. 4): same architecture, merge within models, partial zipping
  - experiments: disjoint sets of CIFAR (cite) and ImageNet (cite) categories; several models from completely independent datasets; significantly beats prior work (Sec. 5)
  - ablation + analysis (Sec. 6)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Since AlexNet made deep learning popular in computer vision, the field has done very well with massive models that have more and more parameters. A lot of vision problems that used to be considered difficult or even impossible are now just benchmark tasks, like classification with tens of thousands of classes, fast instance segmentation, realistic image generation, and more.

There are a lot of independent models out there for many tasks, and they have been carefully tuned. But if we want to expand what an existing model can do, there are many potential issues. If we train the model on an additional task, we get catastrophic forgetting. If we evaluate the same model on different data and don't adapt it, it often does not generalize to out of domain samples. There are so called “intervention” strategies that try to mitigate these effects, but they often need further training, and that can be expensive. It would be better if we could expand a model's capacity to solve new tasks just by “zipping” it with other models trained on those tasks, without any additional training.

Combining multiple models into one has recently started to get attention in the vision community. Model Soups adds multiple models that were finetuned from the same pretrained initialization, which improves accuracy and robustness. Git Re-Basin goes further and handles models trained on the same data but with different initializations, but there is a significant drop in accuracy. REPAIR improves Git Re-Basin by adding new parameters and adjusting the batch norms of the model where applicable. But all of these methods only combine models that were trained on the same task. In this paper we take this line of work to a logical extreme, which is merging differently initialized models that are trained on completely separate tasks (see Fig. 1 ab). We show that this problem is incredibly difficult for prior work, and we use two simple strategies to make it feasible.

- Strategy 1: beyond permutation
  - prior work permutes one model to the other -> 1-1 mapping, assumes most features correlated
  - not necessarily true for different tasks -> permutation alone not enough
  - generalize merging: "zip" any combination of correlated features within and across each model
  - up to 20% better than permutation-based approaches on some tasks
  - proof: merging within models better, theoretical setting of earlier work (cite)

- Strategy 2: partial zipping
  - existing methods merge entire network; ok for extremely similar models, same setting
  - disjoint tasks: features less correlated over the course of the network (cite)
  - zip only up to a specified layer; merged outputs -> remaining unmerged layers of original networks; multi-head model
  - over 15% better depending on task difficulty, most layers still merged

- ZipIt! (Fig. 1 c)
  - zip any number of models from different tasks into one multitask model, no retraining
  - general graph-based algorithm for merging and unmerging (Sec. 4): same architecture, merge within models, partial zipping
  - experiments: disjoint sets of CIFAR (cite) and ImageNet (cite) categories; several models from completely independent datasets; significantly beats prior work (Sec. 5)
  - ablation + analysis (Sec. 6)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Since AlexNet made deep learning popular in computer vision, the field has done very well with massive models that have more and more parameters. A lot of vision problems that used to be considered difficult or even impossible are now just benchmark tasks, like classification with tens of thousands of classes, fast instance segmentation, realistic image generation, and more.

There are a lot of independent models out there for many tasks, and they have been carefully tuned. But if we want to expand what an existing model can do, there are many potential issues. If we train the model on an additional task, we get catastrophic forgetting. If we evaluate the same model on different data and don't adapt it, it often does not generalize to out of domain samples. There are so called “intervention” strategies that try to mitigate these effects, but they often need further training, and that can be expensive. It would be better if we could expand a model's capacity to solve new tasks just by “zipping” it with other models trained on those tasks, without any additional training.

Combining multiple models into one has recently started to get attention in the vision community. Model Soups adds multiple models that were finetuned from the same pretrained initialization, which improves accuracy and robustness. Git Re-Basin goes further and handles models trained on the same data but with different initializations, but there is a significant drop in accuracy. REPAIR improves Git Re-Basin by adding new parameters and adjusting the batch norms of the model where applicable. But all of these methods only combine models that were trained on the same task. In this paper we take this line of work to a logical extreme, which is merging differently initialized models that are trained on completely separate tasks (see Fig. 1 ab). We show that this problem is incredibly difficult for prior work, and we use two simple strategies to make it feasible.

The first strategy comes from noting that prior work focuses on permuting one model to the other one when merging them. This gives a 1-1 mapping between the two models, and that inherently assumes that most of the features across them are correlated. This isn't necessarily true for models trained on different tasks, so permutation alone is not enough. What we do instead is generalize model merging so that it supports “zipping” any combination of correlated features, both within each model and across the models. On some tasks this alone improves accuracy by up to 20% compared to permutation-based approaches. We also prove that merging within models can give a better result in the theoretical setting of an earlier work.

The second strategy is about the fact that existing methods merge the whole network. This might work for models that are extremely similar and trained in the same setting, but for models trained on disjoint tasks the features become less correlated over the course of the network. To solve this we introduce partial zipping, where we only “zip” up to a specified layer. After that, the outputs of the merged model are fed to the remaining unmerged layers of the original networks, which creates a multi-head model. Depending on how difficult the task is, this can improve accuracy by over 15% while most layers are still merged.

Putting both strategies together, we introduce ZipIt! (Fig. 1 c), which is a general method for “zipping” any number of models trained on different tasks into one multitask model without retraining. We derive a general graph-based algorithm for merging and unmerging (Sec. 4), and with it we can zip models of the same architecture together, merge features within each model, and partially zip them to create a multi-task model. To validate the approach we merge models trained on entirely disjoint sets of CIFAR and ImageNet categories, and we also merge several models trained on completely independent datasets into one, and we significantly outperform prior work (Sec. 5). Finally we ablate and analyze the capabilities of our method on these scenarios (Sec. 6).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Ever since AlexNet [1] popularized deep learning in computer vision, the field has thrived with massive models that have an ever increasing number of parameters. Many vision problems once considered difficult or impossible are now benchmark tasks: classification with tens of thousands of classes [2,3,4], fast instance segmentation [5,6], realistic image generation [7,8,9], and more.

There are many independent, carefully tuned models out there for many tasks. However, if we want to expand an existing model’s capabilities, we run into several potential issues. If we try training the model on an additional task, we face catastrophic forgetting [10,11,12]. If we evaluate the same model on different data without adaptation, it often doesn’t generalize to out of domain samples [13,14,15]. So called “intervention” strategies [15,12] can mitigate these effects, but these often require further training, which can be expensive [16,17,18]. Instead, it would be nice to expand a model’s capacity to solve new tasks by simply “zipping” it with other models trained on those tasks without additional training.

Combining multiple models into one has recently started to gain traction in the vision community. Model Soups [19] can add multiple models finetuned from the same pretrained initialization to improve accuracy and robustness. Git Re-Basin [20] generalizes further to models trained on the same data but with different initializations, though with a significant accuracy drop. REPAIR [21] improves on Git Re-Basin by adding new parameters and adjusting model batch norms where applicable. However, all of these methods only combine models trained on the same task. In this paper, we take this line of work to a logical extreme: merging differently initialized models trained on completely separate tasks (see Fig. 1 ab). We show that this is an incredibly difficult problem for prior work and use two simple strategies to make it feasible.

First, we note that prior work focuses on permuting one model to the other when merging them. This creates a 1-1 mapping between the two models, which inherently assumes that most features across them are correlated. Since this isn’t necessarily the case for models trained on different tasks, we cannot rely on permutation alone. Instead, we generalize model merging to support “zipping” any combination of correlated features within and across each model. On some tasks, this alone improves accuracy by up to 20% vs. permutation-based approaches. Moreover, we prove that merging within models can yield a better result in the theoretical setting of [22].

Second, existing methods merge the entire network. This might work for extremely similar models trained in the same setting, but the features of models trained on disjoint tasks become less correlated over the course of the network [23]. To solve this, we introduce partial zipping, where we only “zip” up to a specified layer. Afterward, the merged model’s outputs are fed to the remaining unmerged layers of the original networks, creating a multi-head model. Depending on task difficulty, this can improve accuracy by over 15% while still keeping most layers merged.

Incorporating both of these strategies, we introduce ZipIt! (Fig. 1 c), a general method for “zipping” any number of models trained on different tasks into a single multitask model without retraining. By deriving a general graph-based algorithm for merging and unmerging (Sec. 4), we can zip models of the same architecture together, merge features within each model, and partially zip them to create a multi-task model. We validate our approach by merging models trained on entirely disjoint sets of CIFAR [24] and ImageNet [2] categories, and by merging several models trained on completely independent datasets into one, significantly outperforming prior work (Sec. 5). Finally, we ablate and analyze the capabilities of our method on these scenarios (Sec. 6).
